course.title: Geometry: Shape and Space
course.description: Turn, cut, scale and unfold. Discover how shapes measure the world around you.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with arithmetic, fractions and basic algebra. No previous geometry course is assumed.

lessons.title: Measuring turns

blocks.text: A corner is a turn
A right angle is a quarter-turn: 90°. The marked ray has used 35° of that turn. The remaining part fills the same corner. Compare the 35° and 60° cases; increasing one part must shrink the other.
Along a straight line
A half-turn measures 180°. Adjacent angles on a straight line fill that half-turn, so their measures add to 180°. The unknown angle beside 68° is found by subtraction.
All the way around
A full turn measures 360°. If a pointer turns 140° from its starting direction, it still needs the difference between 360° and 140° to complete one full turn in that direction.
Size of the turn
Angle measures describe rotation, not the length of a ray. The two parts of a straight turn must total 180° even if the drawing is enlarged. An unknown part beside 125° is less than a right angle.

lessons.orientation: Use quarter, half and full turns to find an unknown angle.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Angles in triangles

blocks.text: Three corners, one total
In a flat Euclidean plane, the interior angles of a triangle add to 180°. Changing the triangle's shape changes the individual angles, while their sum stays fixed.
Use the right angle
A right triangle already uses 90° at one corner. Its other two angles must share the remaining 90°. The side across from the right angle is called the hypotenuse.
Equal corners
If two angles of a triangle are equal, subtract the third angle from 180° and split the remainder into two equal parts. For a third angle of 44°, each of the equal angles is 68°.
Check a proposed triangle
Two right angles already use the entire 180° total. That would leave no positive third angle, so a nondegenerate triangle cannot have two right angles. Test a set of angles before drawing it.

lessons.orientation: Find a missing triangle angle and test whether angle measures are possible.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Boundary and area

blocks.text: Fence or floor?

Perimeter counts the boundary length. Area counts how many unit squares cover the inside. A rectangle can share another rectangle's perimeter without sharing its area. Compare the two rectangles and turn on unit squares.
Walk every edge
The opposite sides of a rectangle have equal lengths. A 6 by 4 rectangle has boundary 6 + 4 + 6 + 4, so its perimeter is 20 length units. Count all four edges.
Cover the inside
A 6 by 4 rectangle contains four rows of six unit squares. Its area is 24 square units. Multiplying length by width counts every unit square once.
A different rectangle
A 7 by 3 rectangle has the same perimeter as the 6 by 4 rectangle, but area 21 rather than 24 square units. A fixed amount of fencing does not determine a unique area.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish distance around a shape from the surface it covers.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Base and height

blocks.text: Half a rectangle
A triangle with base 8 and perpendicular height 5 covers half of an 8 by 5 rectangle. Moving the top corner sideways along the same height changes the sloping sides but preserves the area.
Which height counts?

Height is the perpendicular distance to the line containing the base. The dashed guide meets the base at a right angle. A sloping side generally measures a different distance and cannot replace that height.
Pair the triangles

A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two equal-area triangles. Each has half the base-times-height area, so together they cover base times perpendicular height. Sliding the top edge preserves that height.
A new triangle
For base 7 and perpendicular height 6, a triangle covers half of 7 × 6. The equal-area comparison still works when the top corner moves; the formula depends on the base and perpendicular height.

lessons.orientation: Measure perpendicular height and connect triangle area to a parallelogram.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Pieces and cutouts

blocks.text: The missing corner
An L-shaped floor fits inside a 9 by 7 rectangle. The missing corner is 3 by 2. Subtract only that corner from the outer rectangle; the remaining region is the floor.
Two routes, one region

The same L shape can be split into two non-overlapping rectangles: a 9 by 5 lower piece and a 6 by 2 upper piece. Their areas total 57, matching outer area minus cutout. Shared edges are not extra area.
Between two rectangles

A trapezoid has two parallel bases. Its area is their average length times perpendicular height. With bases 10 and 6 and height 4, the area is halfway between the areas of 10 by 4 and 6 by 4 rectangles.
A larger cutout
A 12 by 8 outer rectangle has a 5 by 3 corner removed. Work out the two rectangular areas before subtracting. Removing a bigger corner leaves less area; the outer dimensions alone are not enough.

lessons.orientation: Calculate area by combining simple pieces or subtracting a missing corner.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Around and inside circles

blocks.text: Centre to edge
The radius runs from the centre to the circle. A diameter passes through the centre from edge to edge, so it contains two radii. Show the diameter to compare those distances.
Around the rim
Circumference is the distance around a circle. It equals π times the diameter, or 2π times the radius. With radius 3, the circumference is 6π, approximately 18.84 when using π ≈ 3.14.
Cover the disc
Circle area is π times radius squared. With radius 3, the area is 9π, approximately 28.26 square units when π ≈ 3.14. Circumference and area measure different things and use different units.
Diameter is not radius
A circular mat with diameter 8 has radius 4. Divide the diameter by two before squaring the radius for area. Substituting the diameter as the radius would make the area four times too large.

lessons.orientation: Use radius and diameter correctly in circumference and circle-area calculations.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Same shape, new size

blocks.text: One multiplier
Similar figures have equal corresponding angles and one common ratio between corresponding lengths. A scale factor of 3 changes a width of 2 to 6. The height must use that same factor.
Match corresponding sides
The 3-unit height of the original rectangle becomes 9 under scale factor 3. Match height with height and width with width; mixing those pairs can give the wrong scale factor.
Stretching is different
Applying the same factor to every length preserves the shape. Doubling only the width of a rectangle changes its proportions. Similarity requires all corresponding lengths to share one factor.
A smaller copy
A positive scale factor below 1 produces a smaller copy. With factor 0.5, each length is halved. The direction of the comparison matters: going from the small copy back to the original uses factor 2.

lessons.orientation: Match corresponding lengths and apply one scale factor to every dimension.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: When area scales

blocks.text: Two dimensions change
A 3 by 2 rectangle has area 6. Doubling both lengths makes a 6 by 4 rectangle with area 24. The multiplier appears once in the width and once in the height, producing an area factor of four.
Multiply the multiplier
Tripling every length produces an area factor of 3 × 3 = 9. The original area of 6 becomes 54. This squared factor applies to any similar plane figures.
Use an area you already know
You can scale area without finding every new side. If an original area is 14 and every length is multiplied by 4, multiply 14 by 4². The area grows by sixteen times.
One dimension is not two
Doubling only width gives twice the rectangle's area, while doubling width and height gives four times its area. Check which dimensions actually change before applying the square rule.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish a length scale factor from the resulting area factor.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Right-triangle distances

blocks.text: A shortcut across
For a right triangle, the squares of the two perpendicular legs add to the square of the hypotenuse. With legs 5 and 12, the sum is 25 + 144 = 169. The side length is the positive square root, 13.
Find the hypotenuse
The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side. The theorem is a² + b² = c² when c is the hypotenuse. Relabelling or rotating a triangle does not change that relationship.
Square, add, then root
With legs 6 and 8, calculate 6² + 8² = 100. That is the square of the hypotenuse, not its length. The final square root gives 10. Adding the legs instead measures a bent path.
Work backwards

If the hypotenuse and one leg are known, subtract the known leg's square from the hypotenuse's square. Then take the positive square root. Squared lengths must stay on the correct sides of the equation.

lessons.orientation: Find a missing side using squared lengths and identify when the Pythagorean theorem applies.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Distance on a grid

blocks.text: Read the separation
The points A(1, 2) and B(4, 6) differ by 3 horizontally and 4 vertically. Coordinate differences measure separation; the coordinates themselves measure position relative to the origin.
Two perpendicular legs
Moving horizontally and then vertically makes a right-angle path. Its two lengths can form the legs of a right triangle. The straight segment between the points is the hypotenuse.
Take the straight route
The direct distance uses the square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences. Here √(3² + 4²) = 5. The horizontal-then-vertical route is 7 units long, so it is a different measurement.
Move both endpoints

Adding the same coordinate change to both points translates the segment. Both coordinate differences remain the same, so its length remains the same. Changing position does not necessarily change distance.

lessons.orientation: Use coordinate differences as right-triangle legs and distinguish direct distance from a grid path.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Filling space

blocks.text: Layers of cubes
A rectangular box 4 units long and 3 units wide has room for 12 unit cubes in one layer. Two layers fill a height of 2, giving 24 cubic units. Volume counts space inside.
Add more layers
Keeping the base 4 by 3 while increasing height to 5 gives five layers of 12. Multiplying length, width and height counts the cubes once. The order of these three factors does not matter.
Three dimensions
Volume uses cubic units because each unit cube has length, width and height. Square units measure a surface. A box's capacity and the area of its walls answer different questions.
Scale all three lengths
Doubling all three edges of a cube multiplies volume by 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. A cube of side 3 has volume 27; a cube of side 6 has volume 216. Doubling only height would double volume instead.

lessons.orientation: Count volume in cubic units and predict how it changes when dimensions change.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Unfolding surface area

blocks.text: Unfold the box
A closed rectangular box has six faces. Unfold it to see three pairs: top and base, front and back, left and right. Each pair has equal area, even when its rectangle is turned in the net.
Count every face once
For a 5 by 3 by 2 box, the face areas are 15, 10 and 6, each appearing twice. The total surface area is 2 × (15 + 10 + 6) = 62 square units. Volume would multiply all three lengths instead.
Leave the lid off
An open-top box omits one face. If the top of the 5 by 3 by 2 box is the 5 by 3 rectangle, subtract its area of 15 from the closed total of 62. The required covering area is 47.
Surface or capacity?
Surface area counts square units across the faces; volume counts cubic units inside. In a similar enlargement, doubling every length multiplies each face area by four and volume by eight.

lessons.orientation: Unfold a box to calculate covering area, including the effect of a missing lid.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

questions.prompt: A 90° corner contains a 35° angle. How many degrees remain?
hints: Identify the total turn of the corner.
Subtract the known part from the total.
Calculate 90 − 35.

questions.prompt: Two adjacent angles form a straight line. One is 68°. What is the other, in degrees?
hints: A straight line represents a half-turn.
The adjacent angles add to 180°.
Calculate 180 − 68.

questions.prompt: After turning 140°, how many more degrees complete a 360° turn in the same direction?
hints: Use a full turn as the total.
Find the turn that has not yet been made.
Calculate 360 − 140.

questions.prompt: The rays of an angle are drawn twice as long, without changing direction. What happens to its degree measure?
hints: Separate the length of a ray from its direction.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The degree measure depends on the directions of the rays, so extending them leaves the angle unchanged.

questions.prompt: A right angle is split into 27° and another angle. Find the other angle in degrees.
hints: A right angle is the whole.
Subtract the part already given.
Calculate 90 − 27.

questions.prompt: Which pair can form a straight angle?
hints: Add each pair and compare with a half-turn.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 72° + 108° = 180°, the measure of a straight angle.

questions.prompt: A triangle has angles 48° and 67°. What is its third angle in degrees?
hints: All three interior angles share one fixed total.
Add the two given angles.
Subtract 48 + 67 from 180.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has another angle of 32°. Find its third angle in degrees.
hints: The right angle uses half of the triangle's total.
The two acute angles add to 90°.
Calculate 90 − 32.

questions.prompt: A triangle has two equal angles and a third angle of 44°. Find one equal angle in degrees.
hints: Remove the unequal angle from the total.
Split what remains equally between two angles.
Calculate (180 − 44)/2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The equal angles share 180 − 44 = 136°; each is 136/2 = 68°.

questions.prompt: Can a nondegenerate triangle in a flat plane have two right angles?
hints: Use the sum of the interior angles.

acceptedIdeas: No, that leaves no positive third angle
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two right angles use 180°, leaving 0° for the third; that cannot form a nondegenerate triangle.

choices.label: Yes, if its sides are long enough
No, that leaves no positive third angle
Yes, if its third angle is 90°

questions.prompt: A triangular sign has angles 39° and 86°. Find its third angle in degrees.
hints: Treat all three angles as parts of 180°.
Find the total of the two given angles.
Calculate 180 − (39 + 86).

questions.prompt: Which set can be the interior angles of a triangle?
hints: Check both the total and whether every angle is positive.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 40° + 60° + 80° = 180° and all three measures are positive.

questions.prompt: The rectangles are 6 × 4 and 8 × 2. Which statement is true?
hints: Compare the sum around each boundary with the product of its dimensions.

acceptedIdeas: They have the same perimeter but different areas
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both perimeters are 20, while their areas are 24 and 16 square units.

choices.label: They have the same perimeter but different areas
They have the same area but different perimeters
They have equal areas and equal perimeters

questions.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle 6 units long and 4 units wide.
hints: Perimeter is the total boundary.
There are two sides of each length.
Calculate 2 × (6 + 4).

questions.prompt: Find the area of a rectangle 6 units long and 4 units wide, in square units.
hints: Count square units inside the boundary.
Use the number of rows and squares in each row.
Multiply 6 by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six squares per row across four rows give 6 × 4 = 24 square units.

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 7 units by 3 units. What area does it cover in square units?
hints: Area counts the inside.
Multiply the two perpendicular dimensions.
Calculate 7 × 3.

questions.prompt: A rectangular floor has area 54 m² and width 6 m. Find its length in metres.
hints: Area is length times width.
Undo multiplication by the known width.
Divide 54 by 6.

questions.prompt: Which unit is appropriate for the area of a small floor?
hints: A unit square has both length and width.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Area counts two-dimensional coverage, so it uses square metres.

questions.prompt: A triangle has base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. Find its area in square centimetres.
hints: Compare the triangle with a rectangle of the same base and height.
A triangle covers half that rectangle.
Calculate 8 × 5 / 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Half the enclosing rectangle gives 8 × 5 / 2 = 20 cm².

questions.prompt: The top corner moves sideways but stays 5 cm above an 8 cm base. What happens to the triangle's area?
hints: Identify which dimensions enter the area formula.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The base and perpendicular height remain fixed, so base × height / 2 remains unchanged.

choices.label: It increases with the sloping side

questions.prompt: A parallelogram has base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. Find its area in square centimetres.
hints: A diagonal divides the parallelogram into two triangles.
Adding the two half-areas cancels the division by two.
Calculate 8 × 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two equal-area triangles together cover 8 × 5 = 40 cm².

questions.prompt: Find the area of a triangle with base 7 m and perpendicular height 6 m, in square metres.
hints: Use the base and the perpendicular height.
Take half their product.
Calculate 7 × 6 / 2.

questions.prompt: A triangle has area 42 cm² and base 12 cm. Find its perpendicular height in centimetres.
hints: Reverse the triangle area formula.
Double the area before dividing by the base.
Calculate 2 × 42 / 12.

questions.prompt: Which distance is the height used with a chosen triangle base?
hints: Look for the right-angle relationship to the base.

acceptedIdeas: The perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the base line
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The height must meet the line containing the chosen base at a right angle.

choices.label: The perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the base line

questions.prompt: A 9 m by 7 m floor has a 3 m by 2 m corner removed. Find the remaining area in square metres.
hints: Find the area before removing the corner.
Find the corner's area separately.
Calculate 9 × 7 − 3 × 2.

questions.prompt: You split an L-shaped floor into two rectangles. What must be true before adding their areas?
hints: Check whether any part is missing or counted twice.

acceptedIdeas: They must cover the floor exactly without overlapping
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A disjoint partition counts every part of the floor exactly once.

choices.label: They must overlap as much as possible
They must cover the floor exactly without overlapping

questions.prompt: A trapezoid has parallel bases 10 cm and 6 cm, with perpendicular height 4 cm. Find its area in square centimetres.
hints: Use both parallel bases.
Average their lengths, then multiply by height.
Calculate (10 + 6) × 4 / 2.

questions.prompt: A 12 cm by 8 cm rectangle has a 5 cm by 3 cm corner removed. Find the remaining area in square centimetres.
hints: Treat the missing part as a separate rectangle.
Subtract its area from the full rectangle.
Calculate 12 × 8 − 5 × 3.

questions.prompt: A trapezoid has parallel bases 13 m and 7 m and perpendicular height 5 m. Find its area in square metres.
hints: Area uses the average of the two parallel bases.
Multiply that average by perpendicular height.
Calculate (13 + 7) × 5 / 2.

questions.prompt: Two area pieces overlap in a 4 m² region. Adding their areas counts that region how many times?
hints: Track the overlap once in each piece.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The overlap belongs to both pieces, so the sum counts it twice. Subtract one copy when finding their combined area.

questions.prompt: A circle has radius 3 cm. Find its diameter in centimetres.
hints: The diameter crosses the entire circle through its centre.
It contains a radius on each side of the centre.
Multiply the radius by two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A diameter contains two radii: 2 × 3 = 6 cm.

questions.prompt: A circle has radius 3 cm. Use π ≈ 3.14 to find its circumference in centimetres.
hints: Circumference measures the rim.
Multiply the diameter by π.
Calculate 2 × 3.14 × 3.

questions.prompt: A disc has radius 3 cm. Use π ≈ 3.14 to find its area in square centimetres.
hints: Area covers the disc.
Square the radius, then multiply by π.
Calculate 3.14 × (3 × 3).

questions.prompt: A circular mat has diameter 8 m. Use π ≈ 3.14 to find its area in square metres.
hints: The given distance is the diameter.
Halve it to obtain the radius before squaring.
Calculate 3.14 × (8/2)².

questions.prompt: A radius doubles. What happens to circumference and area?
hints: Compare 2πr with πr².

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Circumference contains one radius factor; area contains two, so their multipliers are 2 and 2².

questions.prompt: Which measurement determines the length of trim around a circular table?
hints: Identify whether you need the boundary or the covered surface.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Trim follows the one-dimensional boundary, so its length is the circumference.

questions.prompt: A 2-unit width is enlarged by scale factor 3. What is the new width?
hints: A scale factor multiplies a length.
Apply it to the corresponding width.
Calculate 2 × 3.

questions.prompt: A similar enlargement uses scale factor 3. An original height is 3 units. What is the new height?
hints: The height uses the same multiplier as the width.
Multiply the original height by the scale factor.
Calculate 3 × 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Every length uses the same factor: 3 × 3 = 9 units.

questions.prompt: Which change guarantees a similar copy of a rectangle?
hints: Similarity uses a common ratio, not a common added amount.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Multiplying every length by the same positive factor preserves angles and proportions.

choices.label: Add 2 units to its width and height

questions.prompt: A 5-unit width is reduced by scale factor 0.5. What is the new width?
hints: A factor below one makes a smaller copy.
Multiplying by one-half halves the width.
Split the original width into two equal lengths.

questions.prompt: On a scale drawing, 1 cm represents 200 cm. A wall is drawn 3 cm long. Find its real length in metres.
hints: First use the drawing-to-real scale factor.
Then convert centimetres to metres.
Calculate (3 × 200)/100.

questions.prompt: Two rectangles have equal areas. What can you conclude about similarity?
hints: Area gives a product, not the ratio of dimensions.

acceptedIdeas: Area alone does not determine whether they are similar
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Different width-to-height ratios can produce the same area. Similarity requires matching proportions.

choices.label: Area alone does not determine whether they are similar

questions.prompt: A 3 cm by 2 cm rectangle has both lengths doubled. Find the new area in square centimetres.
hints: Scale both dimensions before finding area.
Doubling each dimension multiplies area by four.
Calculate (3 × 2) × (2 × 2).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The new rectangle is 6 by 4: 6 × 4 = 24 cm².

questions.prompt: A shape has area 6 cm². Every length is tripled in a similar copy. Find the new area in square centimetres.
hints: Area changes in two dimensions.
Square the length scale factor.
Calculate 6 × 3 × 3.

questions.prompt: A shape has area 14 m². Every length is multiplied by 4 in a similar copy. Find the new area in square metres.
hints: Use the area factor, not just the length factor.
Multiply the original area by the square of four.
Calculate 14 × 4 × 4.

questions.prompt: Only a rectangle's width doubles; its height stays fixed. What is its area factor?
hints: Track which dimensions change.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only one factor in width × height doubles, so the area doubles.

questions.prompt: A similar copy has 9 times the original area. What positive length scale factor was used?
hints: The area factor is the length factor squared.
Reverse squaring with a positive square root.
Find the positive number that multiplies by itself to make 9.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The positive factor whose square is 9 is 3.

questions.prompt: A figure has area 20 cm². A similar copy halves every length. Find the copy's area in square centimetres.
hints: Halving both dimensions gives a quarter of the area.
Multiply the area by one-half twice.
Calculate 20/2/2.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has legs 5 m and 12 m. Find its hypotenuse in metres.
hints: Use the two sides meeting at the right angle.
Square and add the leg lengths.
Take the positive square root of 5² + 12².

questions.prompt: Which side is the hypotenuse of a right triangle?
hints: Locate the right-angle marker first.

acceptedIdeas: The side opposite the right angle
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The hypotenuse lies opposite the right angle, regardless of the triangle's orientation.

choices.label: The side opposite the right angle
Either side touching the right angle

questions.prompt: A right triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find its hypotenuse in centimetres.
hints: The squares of the legs add to the square of the hypotenuse.
Find the sum of 6² and 8².
Take the positive square root of that sum.

questions.prompt: The hypotenuse is c and one leg is a. Which expression gives the other leg's length?
hints: Isolate the square of the missing leg.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: From a² + b² = c², rearrange to b² = c² − a² and take the positive root.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has hypotenuse 25 cm and one leg 7 cm. Find the other leg in centimetres.
hints: The longest side is already known.
Subtract the known leg's square from the hypotenuse's square.
Take the positive square root of 25² − 7².

questions.prompt: A right triangle has perpendicular legs 9 m and 12 m. Find its hypotenuse in metres.
hints: Use squared lengths before finding the side length.
Add the squares of both legs.
Take the positive square root of 9² + 12².

questions.prompt: Points A(1, 2) and B(4, 6) are how many units apart horizontally?
hints: Horizontal position is the first coordinate.
Subtract the two x coordinates.
Find the absolute value of 4 − 1.

questions.prompt: Points A(1, 2) and B(4, 6) are how many units apart vertically?
hints: Vertical position is the second coordinate.
Subtract the two y coordinates.
Find the absolute value of 6 − 2.

questions.prompt: Find the straight-line distance from A(1, 2) to B(4, 6), in grid units.
hints: Use the horizontal and vertical differences as legs.
Add the squares of the differences.
Calculate √((4 − 1)² + (6 − 2)²).

questions.prompt: Both endpoints of a segment move 2 units right and 1 unit up. What happens to its length?
hints: Compare the differences between the endpoints before and after moving.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same translation leaves both coordinate differences unchanged, so the length is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Find the straight-line distance from (−3, 1) to (5, 7), in grid units.
hints: Subtract corresponding coordinates.
The x difference crosses from negative to positive.

questions.prompt: Find the straight-line distance from (−3, −4) to (2, 8), in grid units.
hints: Use coordinate differences, not their sum.
Square the horizontal and vertical separations.

questions.prompt: A rectangular box has inside dimensions 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm. Find its volume in cubic centimetres.
hints: Find the number of unit cubes in one layer.
Multiply by the number of layers.
Calculate 4 × 3 × 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each layer holds 4 × 3 = 12 unit cubes; two layers give 24 cm³.

questions.prompt: A box has inside dimensions 4 cm by 3 cm by 5 cm. Find its volume in cubic centimetres.
hints: Use the base area and height.
The 4 by 3 base is repeated through five layers.
Calculate 4 × 3 × 5.

questions.prompt: Which unit measures how much space is inside a box?
hints: Count the independent dimensions needed to fill the box.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Volume counts three-dimensional unit cubes, so it uses cubic centimetres.

questions.prompt: A cube's side length increases from 3 cm to 6 cm. Find the larger cube's volume in cubic centimetres.
hints: A cube has three equal edge dimensions.
Use the larger side length three times.
Calculate 6³.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The larger cube has volume 6 × 6 × 6 = 216 cm³.

questions.prompt: A storage box has inside dimensions 8 m by 5 m by 4 m. Find its volume in cubic metres.
hints: First find the base area.
Multiply that area by the height.
Calculate 8 × 5 × 4.

questions.prompt: A rectangular box has volume 120 cm³, length 6 cm and width 4 cm. Find its height in centimetres.
hints: Divide volume by the area of one layer.
Find the base area from length and width.
Calculate 120/(6 × 4).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Its base area is 6 × 4 = 24 cm²; height = 120/24 = 5 cm.
